extracted.intended_audience: painters, artists, and students of painting and artistic representation
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and theoretical instructions for painters on depicting the human figure, movement, light, landscape, storms, battles, allegory, group composition, and the scientific principles underlying observation and mechanics. Also includes methodological rules for scientific thought relevant to artistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray figures according to natural proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter should portray his figure according to the measurements of a natural body, which shall be of universal proper proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure yourself and compare to the pattern of excellence; ascertain where your own figure varies and strive to avoid reproducing those defects in figures you portray. Use universal proportions as the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reproducing personal defects in compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contend with all thy might against the fault of reproducing the painter's own bodily defects, since the spirit which governs the body inclines to take pleasure in works similar to itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the part of thy person which is most ugly and, by study, make ample reparation for it; otherwise both the good and ill in thee will be visible in thy compositions (e.g., coarse hands will often be portrayed unless avoided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make figures move—express action convincingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Thou, painter, who knowest not how to make thy figures move, art like the orator who knows not how to employ his words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures must display motion appropriate to the scene; movement gives life and rhetorical power analogous to an orator's use of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match movements to circumstances and age
rubrics_metrics.description: The movements of men are as varied as the circumstances which pass through their minds; an old man or a youth will make a different movement in the same circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose gestures and postures that reflect internal states, strength of circumstances, and age-related physical differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on sight and empirical observation over imagination for visual depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination does not perceive such excellent things as the eye; the eye receives images from objects and transmits them to the perception and brain, whereas imaginative embodiment is born in the dark brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct observation: what the painter sees and records surpasses what poetry or imagination can produce. Use real visual detail rather than relying solely on fanciful invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use painting's visual immediacy to convey what words cannot
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting excels poetry in proportion as the sense to which it ministers is the nobler; the painter can accomplish an infinity of things which speech will not be able to name for want of the appropriate terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit visual richness (e.g., battle scenes, deities, sensuality) to evoke immediate emotional and sensory responses that description alone would struggle to match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base depiction of clouds and atmospheric effects on direct observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe a variety of cloud effects and render them as seen (example: a cloud like a huge mountain full of fiery scales at sunset).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record particulars of lighting, color, scale, and behavior of clouds as observed in nature; small clouds may be attracted to a larger cloud, and cloud lighting varies with sun position and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent vegetation according to soil, moisture, and altitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Grasses and plants will be paler in proportion as the soil is leaner and devoid of moisture; trees will be smaller and thinner as they are nearer the summit of the mountain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On mountain summits show rocks, thin faded moss, small stunted plants, exposed roots; descend toward valleys to depict denser, more vigorous foliage, appropriate species shapes, and varied spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent night scenes by anchoring light sources and color shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: To represent a night subject, represent a great fire so that the nearest objects are tinged with its colour; the object nearest the fire participates most in its nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the fire red and objects nearer appear red; figures between viewer and fire appear dark; side figures half dark/half ruddy; figures beyond flames fully lighted against a black background. Compose actions (shielding faces, raising hands to eyes) to suit glare and heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict storms through disordered, moving elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To represent a storm, show tattered and rent clouds rushing, sandy dust caught up, boughs and leaves torn and dispersed, and people and trees reacting to the wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include bent trees, torn foliage, dust and sand, men fallen or clutching trees, streaming hair and clothes, tempestuous sea with eddies and foam, ships with torn sails and shattered masts, and a dense, terrible air caused by dust, mist, and clouds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render battles with accurate smoke, dust, light, and bodily detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent smoke of artillery mingled with dusty air; dust is earthly and has weight so fine particles rise highest and appear like air-colored haze; smoke assumes bluish colour while dust retains its colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Light should be cast on nearby figures diminishing with distance; figures between viewer and light appear dark against bright background; depict horses with dust clouds proportional to strides; include arrows, smoke trails from cannon-balls, dust clotted on faces, footprints and hoofprints, blood mingled with dust as red mud, varying expressions of agony, and dynamic details like a horse dragging its dead master or riderless horses charging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personify allegorical figures with symbolic attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegorical figures (e.g., Envy, Fame) should be shown with emblematic signs that convey their nature and effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Envy: hands raised in contempt, wounded eye/ear, lean and shrivelled, heart gnawed by a serpent, quiver full of tongues, leopard's skin, vase with flowers and reptiles, riding Death. Fame: rise toward heaven, covered with tongues instead of feathers, depicted as a bird. Use symbolic objects and bodily deformities to communicate moral qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose expressive pictures so spectator reads minds from attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: A picture of human figures should be done so that the spectator can easily recognize the purpose that is in their minds by their attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match gestures to character: a man of high character should have gestures harmonizing with fair words; a man of low character should have fierce gestures and a forward-thrust posture. Use gestures so that even a deaf observer can understand the argument through movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict ages of man with age-appropriate posture and movement
rubrics_metrics.description: How the ages of man should be depicted: infancy, childhood, youth, manhood, old age, decrepitude — each with characteristic posture and movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old men: lazy, slow movements, legs bent, feet parallel and apart, backs bent, heads leaning forward, arms slightly extended. Women: modest attitudes, legs close together, arms folded, head inclined. Old women: eager, vehement, angry gestures with strong arm/head movement. Children: ready, twisted movements when sitting; shy and timid when standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit orator's action to rhetorical mode and depict audience reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: If representing a man talking to many, consider the matter he treats and suit his action to the subject (persuasive, argumentative, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For argumentative matter depict specific hand gestures (e.g., left-hand finger held by two right-hand fingers), mouth half-open, body leaning forward; show the people silent and attentive with varied reactions (old men astonished with mouths pulled down, others clasp hands on knees, bowed men supporting bearded chin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict anger and violence with detailed anatomy and posture
rubrics_metrics.description: An angry man should be shown holding someone by the ear, beating his head against ground, one knee on ribs, right arm raising a fist, hair dishevelled, eyebrows low and narrow, teeth clenched, neck swelled, brow wrinkled and bent forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific facial and bodily tensions to convey fury; coordinate limbs and facial distortion to enhance believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict desperation through visible wounds and frantic posture
rubrics_metrics.description: A desperate man must hold a knife, have torn garments, tear open the wound with one hand, stand with extended feet and slightly bent legs, body leaning to earth, hair flying and dishevelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the violent physicality and self-inflicted wounds to communicate mental state; posture should communicate collapse toward earth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose complex group scenes with distinct, believable small actions
rubrics_metrics.description: In group scenes (example: The Last Supper) individual characters should perform small, telling actions so each gesture contributes to the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use details: one leaves glass and turns head to speaker; another twists fingers, another spreads hands and shrugs with amazement; one whispers in neighbor's ear while holding a knife and bread; one upsets a glass; one puffs cheeks; one shades eyes. Vary spatial relations so gestures interlock and the scene reads naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require mathematical demonstration for true science
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no human experience that can be termed true science unless it can be mathematically demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer disciplines and principles amenable to mathematical demonstration; be skeptical of purely mental sciences that eliminate sensory experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propound theory before explaining practice
rubrics_metrics.description: You must first propound the theory and then explain the practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay out theoretical principles as foundation for subsequent practical instructions or manual work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational principles should be addressed by those with mathematical literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Let no man who is not a mathematician read the principles of my work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical foundations presuppose an understanding of mathematics; ensure readers have sufficient mathematical competence to follow the principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of general rules from prior conclusions permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: In the course of scientific exposition the demonstration of a general rule derived from a previous conclusion is not to be censured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using prior proven conclusions as a basis to derive more general rules is acceptable in exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat mathematics as the standard of certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: He who blames the supreme certainty of mathematics feeds on confusion; no certainty where mathematical sciences cannot be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply mathematical reasoning where possible to silence dispute; regard geometry and arithmetic as exemplars of certain knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base scientific knowledge on sensory experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge which is the issue of experience is termed mechanical; that which is born and ends in the mind is termed scientific; but true and established science must be offspring of experience, mother of all certitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize experimentation and senses; doubt what is contrary to the senses; avoid sciences that do not pass through the five senses and fail to produce established experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics and experience are indispensable to applied science
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics are the paradise of scientific mathematics; experience is indispensable for making any instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanical applications to realize mathematical results; rely on empirical testing when designing instruments or practical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize proportion across domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion is not only to be found in figures and measurements, but also in sound, weight, time and position, and in whatever power which exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider proportional relationships in all aspects of composition, motion, and sensory effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of deceptive or variable experiments; prefer repeated experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The deceptiveness of experiments: those which often appear to be one and the same are often different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on single or purely imagined experiments; repeat observations and test to avoid being misled by appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply understanding of motion, force, inertia, and gravity to depiction and mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects correspond to the force of their cause: a spherical body with a dense superficies will rebound comparably; motion tends to be continuous; force is a power communicated by motion and is origin of gravity; gravity, force, casual motion and resistance are external powers by which visible actions live and die.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these physical principles to inform dynamic depiction (rebound, trajectories, continuity of motion), anatomical rendering of exertion, and the construction of mechanical devices or devices within compositions (e.g., properly rendered motion of thrown objects, falling, or mechanical instruments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Man can imitate instruments governed by mathematical laws but may lack their native power
rubrics_metrics.description: The bird is an instrument which operates by mathematical laws, and man can reproduce all the movements of this instrument, but cannot attain to the intensity of its power; he can acquire balance though not the soul of the bird.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mathematical analysis of natural motion to design imitative devices or to depict motion accurately, while acknowledging physical limitations.
